questions.q: What makes a session token "predictable" rather than secure, in the sense a tester checks for?
options: It is longer than 32 characters
It is only used over HTTPS
It is derived from something guessable, like a sequential integer, timestamp, or hash of the username, instead of coming from a cryptographically secure random generator
It expires after 24 hours
questions.explain: A session token's entire job is being unguessable. If it's built from a sequential ID, timestamp, or a hash of known user data, an attacker can predict rather than steal it, even if it looks random at a glance.

questions.q: How does a tester confirm that a logout button only cleared the cookie client-side without actually invalidating the session server-side?
options: By checking whether the logout button uses a POST request instead of GET
By capturing the session token before logout, then replaying that same captured token against an authenticated endpoint after logging out
By timing how long the logout page takes to redirect
By inspecting the favicon returned after logout
questions.explain: Capturing the token before logout and replaying it afterward against an authenticated endpoint is the direct test: if the server still honors it, the session was never actually revoked server-side.

questions.q: Why is user enumeration a realistic risk in a poorly built password reset flow?
options: Because differences in response time, error text, or status code between a valid and invalid email let an attacker determine which accounts exist before touching a password
Because reset emails are never encrypted in transit
Because password reset flows always expose the database schema directly
Because reset flows require no authentication at all by design
questions.explain: If the app responds differently depending on whether the submitted email exists, an attacker can enumerate every valid account on the system just by observing those response differences.

questions.q: What should happen to a user's other active sessions when that user changes their password?
options: Nothing — only the session that performed the change should ever be affected
All other active sessions for that account should also be invalidated, not just the session that changed it
The account should be permanently locked for 24 hours
All sessions across every account on the platform should be invalidated
questions.explain: A password change should invalidate every other active session tied to that account. Otherwise an attacker who already has an active session keeps access even after the legitimate user changes their password.

questions.q: Which of the following would be considered a critical password reset flow finding during an authorized test?
options: The reset email arrives within 5 seconds of the request
The reset link uses HTTPS
The reset link expires after 10 minutes
The reset token, once issued, is usable against any account rather than being tied specifically to the account it was emailed to
questions.explain: A reset token that isn't tied to the specific account it was issued for — usable against any account — is a critical finding, since it turns the reset flow into a universal account-takeover mechanism.
